course.title: Mechatronics and Robotics
course.description: Microcontrollers, sensors, motors and drivers, state machines and the geometry of robot arms and wheeled robots.
course.audience: Adults who finished Electronics Foundations and know basic programming; no hardware experience needed.

paragraphs: A small DC motor held still on a 12 V supply draws 6 A, while the same motor spinning freely draws almost nothing, because a turning motor is also a generator and pushes back against the supply. Facts like this decide whether a robot works, and they cannot be settled by programming or by mechanics alone. Mechatronics is the engineering of the place where the two meet: the sensors that turn a distance, a temperature or the angle of a shaft into a number, the microcontroller that runs a program on those numbers, and the motors and drivers that turn a number back into force and motion.

Most of the questions the subject asks can be answered with a few lines of arithmetic. A clock frequency and a prescaler tell you how long a timer takes to overflow, the time an echo takes to return tells you how far away a wall is, and the lengths and joint angles of an arm tell you where its hand will be. Once you can do these sums you can read a data sheet and say what a part will do in a design, choose a motor and gearbox that will carry a robot up a slope, and see in advance why a robot that works on the bench might stall on a ramp or reset itself every time its motors start.
outcomes: You'll be able to read a microcontroller's timing and I/O.
You'll be able to convert sensor readings to physical units.
You'll be able to size a motor drive.
You'll be able to compute arm and wheeled-robot kinematics.
introduction.prerequisites: It builds on Electronics Foundations, How Computers Solve Problems and Physics: Motion and Forces.

modules.title: Computers that sense
modules.description: What a microcontroller is, how it reads switches and voltages, and how to structure its behaviour.

modules.title: Making things move
modules.description: DC motors, switching power, steppers, servos and sizing a drive.

modules.title: Robot geometry and behaviour
modules.description: Where a robot is and where its tool is, how sensors are fused, and how a whole robot is organised.

concepts.title: Microcontroller
concepts.summary: A single chip holding a processor, memory and peripherals such as pins, timers and converters, built to read inputs and drive outputs.

concepts.title: Timer
concepts.summary: A counter driven by the clock, optionally slowed by a prescaler, that overflows at a known interval.

concepts.title: Pull-up / pull-down
concepts.summary: A resistor that sets an input to a known level when the switch is open.

concepts.title: Bounce
concepts.summary: A mechanical switch makes and breaks several times in a few milliseconds when pressed.

concepts.title: ADC
concepts.summary: Converts a voltage to an integer of 2^n levels; one step (LSB) is Vref/2^n.

concepts.title: Divider sensing
concepts.summary: A resistive sensor in a divider turns resistance into voltage.

concepts.title: Quadrature encoder
concepts.summary: Two out-of-phase channels give direction and four counts per pulse cycle.

concepts.title: Time of flight
concepts.summary: Distance is half of speed times round-trip time.

concepts.title: Finite state machine
concepts.summary: A set of states, events and a table saying which state follows each event.

concepts.title: Non-blocking timing
concepts.summary: Check elapsed time each pass instead of waiting.

concepts.title: Motor constants
concepts.summary: Torque T = Kt I and back-EMF E = Ke w, equal in SI units.

concepts.title: Stall
concepts.summary: At zero speed there is no back-EMF so current is V/R.

concepts.title: PWM
concepts.summary: Switching a voltage fully on and off; average output = duty x supply.

concepts.title: H-bridge
concepts.summary: Four switches that connect a motor in either direction or brake.

concepts.title: Stepper motor
concepts.summary: Moves in fixed angular steps, 1.8 degrees for 200 steps per revolution.

concepts.title: Servo
concepts.summary: A motor with position feedback; a hobby servo reads a 1 to 2 ms pulse every 20 ms.

concepts.title: Wheel torque
concepts.summary: Force at the ground times wheel radius.

concepts.title: Reflected torque
concepts.summary: Motor torque needed = wheel torque / (ratio x efficiency).

concepts.title: Forward kinematics
concepts.summary: The tool position follows from the joint angles and link lengths.

concepts.title: Workspace
concepts.summary: The set of points the tool can reach; for two links it is a ring.

concepts.title: Inverse kinematics
concepts.summary: Finding joint angles for a given tool position.

concepts.title: Elbow configurations
concepts.summary: Two solutions mirror each other, up and down.

concepts.title: Differential drive
concepts.summary: v = (vr+vl)/2 and w = (vr-vl)/L.

concepts.title: Complementary filter
concepts.summary: Combines gyro (good short term) and accelerometer (good long term).

concepts.title: Sense-plan-act loop
concepts.summary: A repeating cycle with a fixed period.

concepts.title: Power budget
concepts.summary: Battery energy divided by average power gives run time.

lessons.title: What a microcontroller is

lead.text: A **microcontroller** is a single chip that holds a processor, memory and a set of **peripherals**, which are circuits such as pins, timers and converters built in beside the processor. The figure opens one up.

The processor, called the **CPU**, carries out instructions one at a time. The program it follows is kept in **flash** memory, which keeps its contents with the power off, while the variables the program changes live in **RAM**, which does not.

afterFigure.text: The pins are the chip's contact with the world. Each can be made an input, which reads a voltage from a switch or sensor, or an output, which drives an LED or a motor driver.
A microcontroller is therefore *not* a small PC. It has no operating system by default; the program in flash starts when the power comes on and is the only thing that runs.

diagram.alt: A rectangle labelled one chip holding six blocks: CPU, flash, RAM, timer, analog-to-digital converter and pins. Each button highlights one block and says what it does.
diagram.caption: The six parts of a microcontroller, all on one chip. Use the buttons to see what each does.

reveal.text: Flash is written only when new code is uploaded, which is why the program is still there at power-on, while RAM starts empty.
One second divided by 16 million is 62.5 nanoseconds, the time between two ticks.

lead.text: The 16 MHz clock of the previous screen produces a tick every 62.5 nanoseconds, and each tick is called a **cycle**. A simple instruction takes one or a few cycles, so the clock rate sets how much work the chip can do in a second. The figure shows the usual shape of a program on such a chip, written in the Arduino style: `setup` runs once at power-on, and `loop` is run again every time it finishes, for as long as the power lasts.

That repetition is the answer to the question of what the chip does when its program ends, because it never ends. A microcontroller runs one program *forever*, so a program that read a switch once and stopped would never notice the second press. Suppose each pass through `loop` takes 2000 cycles. At 16 MHz the chip completes 16,000,000 / 2000 = 8000 passes every second, so the switch is read every 125 microseconds.

diagram.alt: Arduino-style code with a setup function that runs once and a loop function, highlighted, that repeats for as long as the chip has power.
diagram.caption: The setup function runs once. The loop function runs again as soon as it ends, for as long as there is power.

reveal.text: Halving the work per pass doubles the rate, so the 2000-cycle loop of the text reaches 8000 passes a second.

lead.text: A **timer** is a counter that the clock advances in step. An 8-bit timer holds a number from 0 to 255, adds one on each tick, and after 255 wraps back to 0, an event called an **overflow** that the chip can use to start a piece of code. The time between overflows is fixed by the clock, which is how a chip measures 1 millisecond without the program counting cycles itself.

At 16 MHz an unslowed timer would overflow in only 256 × 62.5 ns = 16 µs, far too fast to be useful for a motor or a display. A **prescaler** divides the clock first, so that the timer ticks once every 64 clock cycles, say. The tick is then 64 × 62.5 ns = 4 µs, and 256 ticks take 256 × 4 µs = 1.024 ms.

afterFigure.text: The relation to remember is *overflow period = counts × prescaler ÷ clock frequency*.

diagram.alt: A clock feeding a divider and then a timer that counts from 0 to 255, with a timeline showing the overflow. Four cases give prescaler 1, 8, 64 and 1024, each with its tick length and overflow time.
diagram.caption: A larger prescaler makes each tick longer, so the same 256 counts take longer. Use the buttons to change the prescaler.

steps.headline: Find the overflow period of an 8-bit timer on an 8 MHz clock with a prescaler of 64.

workedSteps.text: An 8-bit timer counts from 0 up to 255 and then overflows, so one full cycle contains 2^8 ticks.
With the prescaler at 64, one tick lasts 64 clock cycles, and one clock cycle lasts 1 / 8,000,000 s.
The overflow period is the number of ticks multiplied by the length of one tick.
Converted to milliseconds, this is twice the 1.024 ms that the same prescaler gives on a 16 MHz clock, because each clock cycle now lasts twice as long.

steps.headline: Find the overflow period of the same kind of timer back on a 16 MHz clock, with a prescaler of 256.

workedSteps.text: The tick lasts 256 clock cycles.
An 8-bit timer needs 256 ticks to overflow.
The overflow period is the number of ticks multiplied by the length of one tick.

lead.text: The timer from the last screen counts whether or not the CPU is busy, and the same is true of the converter and of the pins' hardware. Each **peripheral** works alongside the CPU, which only has to be told when it has finished. That division of labour is what allows a small, slow chip to keep time, measure a voltage and run a program at once.

The Arduino function `delay(250)` does the opposite: it holds the CPU in a loop for 250 ms and does nothing else meanwhile. A program of the form `readSwitch(); delay(250);` reads its switch only four times a second, so a press shorter than a quarter of a second can fall between two reads. The wait is not free, because the processor is *occupied* for its whole duration.

afterFigure.text: Choosing a part follows from what is on the chip. The questions are how many pins the job needs, how much flash and RAM the program fits in, what speed it must run at, what current the chip draws and what it costs.

reveal.text: Five checks a second is slow enough to miss a short press, which is why later lessons replace waiting with a timer.

lessons.orientation: The parts of a microcontroller, and how its clock and timer give the times a program runs on.
lessons.nextAction: Pick resistor values for a pin that drives an LED, and avoid floating inputs and switch bounce.

blocks.text: The ATmega328P on an Arduino Uno is a chip a little larger than a thumbnail, and it holds a processor, 32 kilobytes of memory for its program and 2 kilobytes for its variables, with no screen, no keyboard and no operating system. When the power comes on it starts a single program, which in a washing machine would read the door switch and the water-level sensor, switch a pump and a motor, and then go back to the start and do it all again, thousands of times a second.

A chip of this kind is called a **microcontroller**, and it is the part that turns a collection of motors and sensors into a machine that behaves. It keeps time with a clock, which on the Uno ticks 16 million times a second, so every delay the machine produces is a count of those ticks.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to name the parts of a microcontroller and work out how long a timer takes to overflow from its clock and prescaler.
intro.whyItMatters: Every later lesson, from sensors to motors, relies on knowing how fast the chip runs and how it keeps time.

recap.keyIdea: A microcontroller is a whole computer on one chip that runs one program forever, and its clock and timers turn cycles into known times.

blocks.text: The CPU, the flash, the RAM, the timer, the converter and the pins sit on one piece of silicon, and the program in flash starts at power-on and loops until the power goes. The clock sets the length of a cycle, and a timer, slowed by a prescaler, turns cycles into a regular overflow such as 1.024 ms.
Because the peripherals work beside the CPU, a program should let them do the timing and not hold the CPU in a delay, which would leave the inputs unread.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson connects the pins to the world, choosing resistors for LEDs and handling switches that float or bounce.

lessons.title: Digital pins, switches and LEDs

lead.text: Every pin of a microcontroller is set by the program to be an **input** or an **output**. An output pin connects the chip's supply voltage or ground to whatever is attached, so it can light an LED. An input pin does the reverse and only *measures*: the voltage on it is compared with a threshold, and anything above the threshold reads as **high**, which the program sees as 1, while anything below reads as **low**, or 0.

The thresholds depend on the supply. On a chip such as the ATmega328P they sit at about 0.3 and 0.6 of the supply voltage, so on a 5 V part a voltage under about 1.5 V reads low and one over about 3 V reads high, and a voltage in between is not guaranteed to read as either. A 3.3 V part has lower thresholds.

afterFigure.text: Each pin can also supply only a limited current, of the order of 20 mA on the Arduino Uno.

reveal.text: With nothing driving it the pin is not at 0 V and not at the supply either. Its voltage drifts with stray charge and noise, and the next screen shows how to fix it.

lead.text: A pin that is connected to nothing is said to **float**. Its input is so sensitive that it picks up the mains hum from nearby wiring and the touch of a finger, so the program may read high or low and change its answer from one pass of the loop to the next. The cure is to give the pin a path to a known level when the switch is open.

A **pull-up resistor** joins the pin to the supply through a large resistance, such as 10 kΩ. With the switch open almost no current flows, so there is almost no voltage across the resistor and the pin sits at the supply, which reads high. When the switch closes it joins the pin to ground, which wins easily because the resistor limits the current, and the pin reads low. A **pull-down** resistor does the same job the other way round, holding the pin low until a switch connects it to the supply.

afterFigure.text: Because the resistor is large, the pressed switch wastes little current: by [[Ohm's law|V = I × R. Met in Electronics Foundations.]], the 10 kΩ resistor with 3.3 V across it passes 3.3 V / 10,000 Ω = 0.33 mA. Many microcontrollers have such resistors built into their pins, enabled in software, so that no part has to be added.

reveal.text: A milliamp and a half is still small, but a 10 kΩ pull-up passes less than a quarter of it, which is why large pull-up values are usually chosen.

lead.text: An LED is not like a resistor: once the voltage across it passes its **forward voltage**, about 2 V for a red one, the current through it rises very steeply, and nothing in the LED limits it. The remedy is a resistor in series, which takes up the voltage the LED cannot use.

The voltage across the resistor is the supply minus the LED's forward voltage, and the current through the two is the same because they are in series, so Ohm's law gives the resistor: *R = (Vs − Vf) / I*. For a 5 V pin, a 2 V LED and a wanted current of 15 mA this is 3 V / 0.015 A = 200 Ω.

afterFigure.text: Resistors are sold in standard values, so the calculated value is usually rounded to the next one *up*, which gives a slightly smaller current and a slightly dimmer LED but never an overload.

steps.headline: Choose a resistor for a green LED, 2.2 V forward voltage, run from a 5 V pin at 8 mA.

workedSteps.text: The resistor must take whatever the LED does not. Subtract the forward voltage from the supply.
The same 8 mA flows through the resistor, so Ohm's law gives its value.
Work out the division.
Check the other way: with 350 Ω the current is the voltage over the resistance, which is the 8 mA that was asked for.

steps.headline: Choose a resistor for a blue LED, 3.2 V forward voltage, run from a 5 V pin at 10 mA.

workedSteps.text: The resistor must take the supply minus the forward voltage.
The same 10 mA flows in the resistor, which is 0.010 A.
Ohm's law gives the resistor from the voltage across it and the current through it.

lead.text: The common E12 range of resistor values has no 200 Ω, so the next standard value up, 220 Ω, is fitted instead.

reveal.text: The current is 13.6 mA, a little under the 15 mA planned, so the LED is slightly dimmer and well within its limit.

lead.text: Inside a push button, a metal contact meets another and rebounds slightly before it settles, as a dropped coin does on a table. For a few milliseconds, typically around 5, the voltage at the pin flips between high and low many times before it stays low. This is called **bounce**.

A program that counts the edges at the pin would count a single press as several, so a counter that should go up by one goes up by three or four. The extra edges are real changes of voltage, not a fault of the chip, so the cure is in the program.

afterFigure.text: The usual cure is to **debounce** the input: after a change is noticed, ignore further changes for a short time, longer than the bounce. A program that checks the pin every 10 ms, for a bounce of about 5 ms, will in practice see the press once, because by the time of the next look the contact has settled. The 5 ms is a typical value and not a guaranteed one, so a design leaves a margin.

A smaller pull-up holds the pin more firmly against noise but wastes more power whenever the button is pressed, so 10 kΩ is a common compromise.

lessons.orientation: How a pin reads or drives a voltage, why inputs need pull-ups, how to size an LED resistor and how to debounce a switch.
lessons.nextAction: Convert a voltage read by the analog-to-digital converter into a number and back.

blocks.text: A push button wired between an input pin and ground looks like the simplest input a microcontroller can have, since the program only has to ask whether the pin is high or low. A first attempt rarely behaves, though, and a single press is often counted three or four times, because a pin is a comparator on a voltage and a switch is a piece of metal, and neither is as tidy as the program assumes.

Getting it right takes a resistor that gives the pin a defined level and a short wait in the software that sees past the moment the contacts meet. The output side needs the same care, since an LED wired straight to a pin can burn out, and with Ohm's law and a few resistors chosen correctly you can connect any switch or indicator to a chip and trust what the program reads from it.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to choose an LED resistor, say why an input needs a pull-up and explain how a program deals with switch bounce.
intro.whyItMatters: Almost every sensor and actuator reaches the chip through pins, so their electrical limits decide whether a design works.

recap.keyIdea: A pin needs defined voltages and limited current: a pull-up gives an input a level, a series resistor limits an LED, and software ignores a switch's bounce.

blocks.text: An input left unconnected floats and reads noise, so a pull-up or pull-down resistor fixes its level when the switch is open. An LED needs a series resistor of (Vs − Vf) / I, and a real switch bounces for a few milliseconds, so the program should ignore changes for a short time after the first.
The numbers in this lesson, 200 Ω for a red LED on 5 V and 0.33 mA through a 10 kΩ pull-up on 3.3 V, are the pattern for every pin you connect.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson reads a voltage that is not simply high or low, using the analog-to-digital converter.

lessons.title: Analog signals and the converter

lead.text: A sensor's voltage can take any value between 0 V and the supply, but a microcontroller works with whole numbers. The **analog-to-digital converter**, or **ADC**, bridges the two by dividing the range from 0 V up to a **reference voltage** Vref into equal steps and reporting which step the input falls in. An *n*-bit converter has 2^n steps, so a 12-bit one has 4096 and a 10-bit one has 1024.

The size of one step is the **least significant bit**, written LSB, and it is Vref / 2^n. A 12-bit converter with a 3.3 V reference has LSB = 3.3 / 4096 = 0.806 mV, and a 10-bit converter with a 5 V reference has LSB = 5 / 1024 = 4.88 mV. Every voltage inside a step gives the same count.

afterFigure.text: The number the program receives is therefore a *count*, and turning it into volts is a calculation the program must do. More bits make the steps finer, but they do not make the reading *accurate*: the result is only as good as the reference voltage and the noise on the input, and a 12-bit reading taken against a reference that is 2% wrong is 2% wrong at any number of bits.

diagram.alt: A sine wave drawn in grey with a blue staircase approximating it. Three cases use 2, 3 and 4 bits, giving 4, 8 and 16 levels, and the staircase follows the wave more closely each time.
diagram.caption: More bits give more, finer steps, and the staircase follows the voltage more closely. Use the buttons to change the bits.

reveal.text: The count says how far up the scale the voltage lies, and 256 is a quarter of 1024, so the voltage is a quarter of the 5 V reference, about 1.25 V.

lead.text: The voltage is the count times the size of one step: *V = count × Vref / 2^n*. The reverse uses the same step: *count = V × 2^n / Vref*, rounded down to a whole number because the converter reports only the step the voltage lies in. With a 12-bit converter and Vref = 3.3 V, a reading of 2048 means 2048 × 3.3 / 4096 = 1.650 V.

A program on an Arduino Uno shows the same arithmetic. The call `int n = analogRead(A0);` returns a number from 0 to 1023, which is a 10-bit reading, and `float v = n * 5.0 / 1024.0;` turns it into volts for the 5 V reference.

afterFigure.text: The largest count is 2^n − 1, not 2^n, so a voltage at the very top of the range reads 4095 on a 12-bit converter. The slight mismatch is why some programs divide by 4095 and some by 4096; the difference is under 0.03% and does not matter for the examples here.

steps.headline: A 12-bit converter with Vref = 3.3 V returns 2560. What voltage is on the pin?

workedSteps.text: Find the size of one step first: the reference divided by the number of steps.
The voltage is the count times that step.
Work out the product and give it in volts.

steps.headline: A 10-bit converter with Vref = 5 V returns 300. What voltage is on the pin?

workedSteps.text: One step is the reference divided by 2^10 = 1024 steps.
The voltage is the count times one step.

reveal.text: The count is 204, because 204.8 lies in the step numbered 204, and a converter reports only the step.

lead.text: Many sensors change their *resistance* and not a voltage. A **thermistor** is a resistor whose resistance falls as it warms. The converter cannot read a resistance, so the sensor is put in a **voltage divider** with a fixed resistor, as in the figure, and the voltage at the middle node depends on how the supply divides between the two.

With the fixed resistor R on the top and the sensor Rt below it, the node voltage is *Vout = Vs × Rt / (R + Rt)*. Cool, the 10 kΩ thermistor is equal to R and the node sits at half the supply, 1.65 V. Warm, at 5 kΩ, it falls to 3.3 × 5 / 15 = 1.10 V, which the 12-bit converter reads as a count of about 1365.

afterFigure.text: The relation can be turned round, and that is how a program recovers the sensor's resistance from its reading: *Rt = R × Vout / (Vs − Vout)*. A further table or formula then turns resistance into temperature.

diagram.alt: A thermistor divider: 3.3 volts, a 10 kilohm resistor, a node connected to an ADC pin, and the thermistor to ground. Two cases show a cool thermistor of 10 kilohms and a warm one of 5 kilohms.
diagram.caption: The thermistor is the lower part of a divider. When it warms its resistance falls and so does the voltage at the pin.

reveal.text: A smaller thermistor takes a smaller share of the supply, so the warmer it is the lower the voltage at the pin.

steps.headline: A 12-bit converter with Vref = 3.3 V, on the divider above, returns 3072. Find the thermistor's resistance.

workedSteps.text: The count is 3072 of 4096, which is three quarters of the reference.
The rearranged equation also needs the voltage across the fixed resistor, which is what the thermistor leaves of the supply.
The thermistor and the fixed resistor divide the supply in the ratio of their resistances.

lead.text: Real readings jitter by a count or two even when the voltage is steady, because of noise in the sensor, the supply and the converter. This noise is *random*, which means that it is as likely to push a reading up as down, so averaging N readings lets the errors cancel in part. The random noise falls by a factor of √N: 16 samples cut it to a quarter and 64 to an eighth, as the figure shows.
Averaging has limits. A reference voltage that is wrong by 2% makes every sample wrong in the same direction, and no number of samples averages that away.

afterFigure.text: Time matters in a second way. A converter takes a reading, waits, and takes another, so a voltage that rises and falls between two readings is simply missed. The rule is to sample at least *twice* as fast as the fastest change that you need to see, a result known as the Nyquist rate.

diagram.alt: Four bars for N equal to 1, 4, 16 and 64 samples averaged, with random noise at 1, one half, one quarter and one eighth of the single-sample value.
diagram.caption: Each quadrupling of the samples halves the random noise. The numbers are relative to a single reading.

reveal.text: The same arithmetic runs in every sketch that reads a sensor, so the faulty line in a program that reads wrongly is often a wrong divisor.
The noise falls as the square root of the number of readings, so 100 readings cut it by a factor of 10.

lessons.orientation: How a converter turns a voltage into a count, how a divider lets it read a resistance, and what noise does.
lessons.nextAction: Compute distance from an encoder and from a time-of-flight sensor, and choose the right sensor.

blocks.text: A converter on a microcontroller hands the program a reading of 2048, and the number carries no unit. It is a position on a scale that runs from 0 V up to a reference voltage, so with a 3.3 V reference on a 12-bit converter this reading stands for 1.650 V, while against a 5 V reference it would stand for 2.5 V.

Every sensor on a robot reaches the program in this form, as a count, and many sensors do not produce a voltage in the first place, since a thermistor changes its resistance as it warms. Turning a count back into volts, and volts back into the resistance of a sensor, is therefore the first step of any measurement.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to convert between a converter's count and a voltage, recover a sensor's resistance from its divider, and say how much averaging reduces noise.
intro.whyItMatters: Every sensor on a robot reaches the program as a count, so converting it correctly is the first step of control.

recap.keyIdea: A converter reports a voltage as a count of 2^n steps of size Vref / 2^n, and a divider lets it read a resistance.

blocks.text: A count converts to a voltage by multiplying by Vref / 2^n, and a resistive sensor in a divider turns its resistance into a voltage that the equation Rt = R × Vout / (Vs − Vout) turns back again. More bits give finer steps, but the reference and the noise limit the accuracy.
Averaging N readings cuts random noise by √N, but not a fixed error such as a wrong reference, and the sampling must be at least twice as fast as the changes to be seen.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson turns to sensors for position and motion, where a count is converted into a distance.

lessons.title: Sensors for position and motion

lead.text: A sensor is described by a few numbers. Its **range** is the span it can measure, its **resolution** is the smallest change it can report, its **accuracy** is how close the reading is to the true value, its **noise** is the scatter between readings of an unchanged quantity, and its **speed** is how often it can report. They are different properties: a sensor can have fine resolution and poor accuracy, as a converter with a wrong reference does.
A robot's program should therefore treat a reading as an *estimate* with a size of error, and not as the quantity itself.

reveal.text: Each pulse cycle contains four edges, two on channel A and two on channel B, so 600 cycles give 2400 counts.

lead.text: A **quadrature encoder** is a disc with fine slots that turns with a wheel or a motor shaft, read by two sensors placed so that their signals, channel A and channel B, are a quarter of a cycle out of step. As the disc turns, each channel produces a square wave.

The two waves give direction. When A rises before B the disc is turning forward, and when B rises before A it is turning backward, because the quarter-cycle offset makes the sequence of the two reverse with the direction. The chip also gets more than one count from each slot: each cycle contains four edges, a rising and a falling one on each channel, so counting them all, called **4× counting**, gives four **counts** per pulse cycle.

afterFigure.text: Be careful with the units on a data sheet. The encoder's rating is in **pulses per revolution**, or PPR, which counts cycles of one channel, while the program counts *edges*. A 600 PPR encoder therefore gives 2400 counts per revolution, and one count is 360° / 2400 = 0.15° of turn.

diagram.alt: Two square-wave channels A and B a quarter of a cycle apart. When A rises first the disc turns forward and when B rises first it turns backward. A third case numbers the four edges in one cycle.
diagram.caption: The order of the two channels gives the direction, and every edge is a count. Use the buttons to compare.

steps.headline: A 400 PPR encoder with 4× counting is on a wheel of 80 mm diameter. How far does the wheel travel in 4800 counts?

workedSteps.text: Counts per revolution are four times the pulses per revolution.
One revolution carries the wheel once round its circumference, π × d.
The distance per count is the circumference divided by the counts per revolution.
Travel is the number of counts times that distance.

steps.headline: A 1000 PPR encoder with 4× counting is on a wheel of 100 mm diameter. How far does the wheel travel in 12,000 counts?

workedSteps.text: Counts per revolution are four times the pulses per revolution.
The circumference is π times the diameter.
The wheel moves one circumference for each full revolution that the counts add up to.

lead.text: A **time-of-flight** sensor sends a pulse, waits for its reflection and times the gap. An ultrasonic one uses a burst of sound at a frequency above hearing, and the speed of sound in air at 20 °C is about 343 m/s. The sound travels to the wall *and back*, so the time covers twice the distance: *d = v × t / 2*.
For an echo of 5.8 ms the sound has travelled 343 × 0.0058 = 1.99 m, and the wall is half of that, 0.995 m away. Leaving out the halving is the common error, and it doubles every reading.

afterFigure.text: The speed of sound rises by about 0.6 m/s for each degree Celsius, so a sensor that assumes 343 m/s is about 3% out on a day that is 15 °C warmer. A reading also has a range: below a few centimetres the echo comes back before the sensor is ready, and a soft or angled surface returns almost none.

diagram.alt: A robot sends a ping to a wall and receives the echo. One case shows the path out and back with a 5.8 millisecond round trip. The other halves speed times time to give 0.995 metres.
diagram.caption: The echo time covers the distance twice, so halve it. Use the buttons to see the path and the sum.

reveal.text: The 8.7 ms is the round trip, and the object is at half of the distance the sound covered.

lead.text: Readings of an unchanged distance scatter, and the usual remedy is to average a few of them. The scatter falls, but the average also *lags*: when the true distance drops from 100 cm to 90 cm the average takes several readings to catch up. Smoothness is bought with delay, and a robot that is moving quickly may not be able to afford it.

The inertial sensors have a worse problem. A **gyroscope** measures how fast something is turning, a rate in degrees per second, and an **accelerometer** measures acceleration. Neither reports position or angle, and to get an angle the program must add up the rate over time. A small constant error in the rate, a **bias**, is added up too: a gyroscope with a bias of 0.5°/s gives an angle that is wrong by 0.5 × 60 = 30° after one minute.

afterFigure.text: The error grows without limit, which is why a later lesson uses a second sensor to correct it.

diagram.alt: A distance sensor reading 100 centimetres that steps down to 90. Raw readings scatter by a few centimetres. A five-reading average is smoother but follows the step after a short lag.
diagram.caption: Averaging smooths the scatter and delays the response. Use the buttons to compare.

reveal.text: Because the angle is a sum, a rate error grows as time passes, and this is the reason inertial sensors need an outside check.
The encoder measures the wheel's own rotation, so unlike a gyroscope it does not need its output added up over time to give distance.

lessons.orientation: How encoder counts and echo times become distances, and what each sensor can and cannot report.
lessons.nextAction: Describe a program as a state machine, trace it step by step and count its transitions.

blocks.text: An encoder on a robot's wheel is a disc of 600 slots that turns between a light and a pair of sensors, and as the wheel turns the chip counts the edges of the pulses that the sensors produce. After a short run it might have counted 7200 edges, which is only a number until the program turns it into a distance, and for a wheel 65 mm across that means knowing exactly how many counts make one turn and how far one turn carries the robot, which here comes to 612.6 mm.

An ultrasonic sensor measures distance in a different way, by sending out a click of sound and timing its echo, so that a gap of 5.8 ms means a wall 0.995 m away. One sensor counts and the other times, and both give estimates with some scatter.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to turn encoder counts and echo times into distances and choose a sensor for a measurement.
intro.whyItMatters: A robot that cannot measure how far it has moved cannot steer, and these two conversions are the commonest way to find out.

recap.keyIdea: Encoder counts times the distance per count, or half the echo time times the speed of sound, give distance, and each sensor has noise and a limit.

blocks.text: A quadrature encoder gives four counts per pulse cycle and the order of its channels gives direction, so counts multiplied by distance per count give travel. An echo gives distance as half of the speed of sound times the round-trip time.
Both readings are estimates: averaging reduces scatter but adds lag, and a gyroscope's angle drifts because it adds up a rate with a bias.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson organises a robot's behaviour into states, so that a program can decide what to do with these readings.

lessons.title: State machines

lead.text: A vending machine reacts to the same button press in different ways. With no money in it the press does nothing, and with the coin inserted the press releases the drink. The input is the same, and the difference lies in what happened earlier, which the machine has to remember. A program built round this idea is a **finite state machine**, made of a fixed set of **states**, the situations the machine can be in, and **events**, the things that can happen to it.

The figure shows a machine with three states: idle, run and pause. The press event takes it from idle to run, a second press to pause, and a reset from pause back to idle. Each arrow is a **transition**, and the machine is in exactly one state at a time, shown here by the highlighted circle.

afterFigure.text: Because only one state is current, the behaviour cannot contradict itself. A program that tracks the same situation with several yes-or-no flags, such as running, paused and stopped, can end up with two of them set at once, and no line of code will say which is right. One state variable has no such disagreement.

diagram.alt: A state diagram with three states: idle, run and pause. Arrows show press from idle to run, press from run to pause, press from pause to run, timeout from run to idle and reset from pause to idle. Four cases follow the events press, press, reset.
diagram.caption: The current state is highlighted. Use the buttons to follow the events press, press, reset.

reveal.text: A timeout has nothing to end while the machine is idle, so the sensible choice is to ignore it and stay in idle, and the next screen shows how a table records that.

lead.text: The arrows of a state diagram can be written as a **transition table**. Its rows are states, its columns are events, and each cell names the state that follows. The figure holds the table of the machine on the previous screen.

Only five of the nine cells are filled. The others are *not* mistakes, because a machine does not have to respond to every event in every state: a timeout means nothing to a machine that is idle. A blank cell means that the event is ignored and the state stays as it is, and it is a **design decision** that should be made on purpose, not by omission.

afterFigure.text: With *s* states and *e* events a table has at most s × e cells, which is a quick check on a design. Four states and three events give at most 12 transitions, and in practice many cells are blank.

diagram.caption: Every cell is one state and one event. A blank cell means the machine stays where it is. Use the buttons to mark the blank cells.

steps.headline: Starting in idle, trace the events press, press, reset through the table.

workedSteps.text: Start in the state idle.
The first event is press, and the table says idle + press gives run.
The second event is press, and run + press gives pause.
The third event is reset, and pause + reset gives idle.

steps.headline: Starting in idle, trace the events press, press, press through the same table.

workedSteps.text: Start in idle. The first press gives run.
The second press gives pause.
The third press arrives in pause, and the table's pause + press cell gives the final state.

lead.text: The table becomes a program in a very direct way. The Python version holds the table as a dictionary whose keys are the pairs (state, event), and the loop runs `s = table.get((s, e), s)` for each event. The second argument is the value to use if the pair is not in the table, and passing the current state *s* is what makes a blank cell leave the state unchanged.

On a microcontroller the same machine is written with a single variable, often a switch (state) with a case for each state, and an if on the event inside it. The variable is the only place that remembers the history, so there is nothing to keep in step.

reveal.text: The reset arrives while the machine is in run, where the table has no cell for it, so the default keeps the state.

lead.text: Suppose the pause state must last one second. The obvious code calls `delay(1000)`, and during that second the processor does nothing else, so a button pressed and released within it is never seen, as the figure shows. A state machine is only useful if it looks at its events all the time.

The remedy is to check the clock instead of waiting. The program records the time when the state was entered, `start = millis();`, where `millis()` returns the milliseconds since the chip started, and on every pass it asks `if (millis() - start >= 1000)`. The loop keeps running, so it reads the button on every pass, and the timeout becomes one more event that the table handles.

afterFigure.text: The check happens only once per pass. If a pass takes 30 ms, the elapsed time is looked at at 30 ms, 60 ms and so on, so a 1000 ms timeout is noticed at the first pass at or beyond 1000 ms, which is 1020 ms.

diagram.alt: A timeline from 0 to 1500 milliseconds with a button press from 400 to 500. With delay(1000) the program is waiting and the press is missed. With checks every 50 milliseconds the press is seen.
diagram.caption: Waiting hides a press that falls inside the wait. Use the buttons to compare.

lead.text: A machine that drives motors should have a state in which it is harmless: motors off, brakes on, outputs at rest. Call it *safe*. A fault event, such as an obstacle sensor or a stalled motor, should lead to it from **every** other state, so that nothing the robot is doing can fail to stop it.

In a table this is a column of entries, one per state, and all of them lead to the same place. It is also why blank cells should be chosen deliberately: for a fault event no cell may be blank, whereas for most other events the blank cell is the right answer.

afterFigure.text: A traffic light shows the pattern. Its states red, green and yellow follow each other on a timer event, which is three transitions, and a fault event sends each of the three to a fourth state, flashing red. That adds three more, so six transitions are listed in a table that has room for eight.

reveal.text: A fault can arrive in any state, so every state other than halted needs a fault cell that leads to halted, and a blank cell would leave the controller carrying on as if nothing had gone wrong.

lessons.orientation: How to describe behaviour as states, events and a transition table, trace it, and keep it from waiting.
lessons.nextAction: Compute the stall torque, no-load speed and operating point of a DC motor.

blocks.text: A garage door opener responds to its one button in several different ways. Pressed while the door is closed it starts the motor upward, pressed while the door is moving it stops it, and pressed while the door is stopped it sets it off the other way, so what a press means is a property of what has already happened and not of the button, and the controller has to remember it.

A program that keeps that memory in a handful of separate flags soon contradicts itself, with one flag saying the door is moving and another saying it has stopped. A **finite state machine** keeps all of the memory in one variable and lists, for each situation and each event, what happens next.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to trace a state machine through a table of events, count its transitions and write its waits without delay().
intro.whyItMatters: Every robot program of any size is organised this way, because its behaviour depends on what has already happened.

recap.keyIdea: A state machine holds a robot's history in one state variable, moves on events by a transition table, and ignores unlisted events on purpose.

blocks.text: The states and events give a table of at most states × events moves, in which a blank cell means the machine stays put. In code it is one variable and one lookup, and a wait is written as a check of the elapsed time so that events are never missed.
A safe state, reached from every state by a fault event, makes sure that a failure ends somewhere harmless.

lessons.title: DC motors

lead.text: A DC motor turns electrical power into rotation, and it also runs in reverse: spun by hand, it produces a voltage. That voltage is present whenever the shaft turns, including when the motor is being driven, where it opposes the supply and is called the **back-EMF**. It is proportional to the angular speed ω, in radians per second, *E = Ke ω*, where Ke is a constant of the motor.

The torque the motor produces is proportional to the current through its winding, *T = Kt I*. For a motor in SI units the two constants have the same value, so a motor with Kt = 0.05 N m/A has Ke = 0.05 V s/rad. Speed in rad/s is related to revolutions per minute by ω = rpm × 2π / 60, so 1000 rpm is 104.7 rad/s.

afterFigure.text: The supply must push current through the winding resistance R against this back-EMF, so the current is *I = (V − E) / R*. The figure puts numbers to it for a 12 V supply and a winding of 2 Ω: the faster the motor turns, the larger E is and the smaller I becomes, until at 240 rad/s the two voltages match and no current flows.

diagram.alt: A series loop of a 12 volt supply, a 2 ohm winding resistance and a motor whose back-EMF opposes the supply. Three cases at 60, 120 and 240 radians per second show the current falling from 4.5 amps to 0.
diagram.caption: As the motor speeds up its back-EMF rises and the current falls. Use the buttons to change the speed.

reveal.text: With no turning there is no back-EMF, so the whole 12 V falls across the winding and the current is 12 / 2 = 6 A.

lead.text: A motor that is not turning has no back-EMF, so the whole supply voltage falls across the winding resistance. That state is called **stall**, and the **stall current** is V / R, which is 12 / 2 = 6 A for the motor of the figure. The torque there is Kt × I = 0.05 × 6 = 0.30 N m, the largest the motor can give, and it falls in a straight line as the speed rises.

At the other end, a motor with nothing to turn speeds up until its back-EMF almost equals the supply. This **no-load speed** is V / Ke, which is 12 / 0.05 = 240 rad/s, or 2292 rpm, and the current there is almost zero because there is no longer a voltage to push it.

afterFigure.text: The power the motor delivers is torque times speed, and it is zero at both ends, since one factor is zero at each. The peak lies at half the no-load speed, 120 rad/s, where the torque is 0.15 N m and the power 18 W. A motor current is therefore *not* constant: it follows the load, from 6 A at a standstill to almost nothing when free.

reveal.text: A smaller Ke means a smaller back-EMF at a given speed, so the motor has to turn faster to reach 12 V.

steps.headline: The 12 V motor (R = 2 Ω, Kt = Ke = 0.05) turns at 1500 rpm. Find the current and the torque.

workedSteps.text: Convert the speed from revolutions per minute to radians per second.
The back-EMF is Ke times the speed.
The voltage left across the winding drives the current.
The torque is Kt times the current.

steps.headline: The same motor turns at 1200 rpm. Find the current.

workedSteps.text: Convert the speed to radians per second.
The back-EMF is Ke times the speed.
The voltage that the back-EMF leaves across the winding drives the current through the winding resistance.

lead.text: At stall the motor draws 12 V × 6 A = 72 W and delivers no mechanical power at all, because nothing moves. All 72 W goes into the winding as heat, which equals I² R = 36 × 2 = 72 W. A stalled motor is therefore far from safe: a small winding is not built to shed that much heat, and a robot that drives into a wall with its motors still powered can burn them out.

Efficiency is the mechanical power divided by the electrical power drawn. At stall it is zero, and it grows with speed because the back-EMF, which is useful work, takes a larger share of the supply. In the ideal motor used here it is simply ω Ke / V, 50% at half the no-load speed and 75% at three quarters. Real motors also lose power to friction, which pulls the best efficiency to a high fraction of no-load speed, but never at stall.

afterFigure.text: The lesson for design is to choose a motor so that it runs in the middle of its line, with some headroom, and to limit the current or cut the power when a motor stalls.

reveal.text: Forty-eight watts in a winding that is built for a fraction of it is why stall protection matters.
Power is torque times speed, so it is zero at stall and at no load, and for this lesson's motor it peaks at 18 W at half the no-load speed.

lessons.nextAction: Control a motor's speed with pulse-width modulation, and choose an H-bridge to drive it in both directions.

blocks.text: A small DC motor connected to 12 V spins up to 240 rad/s in a fraction of a second, and its winding, a coil of copper wire with a resistance of only 2 Ω, is the same piece of wire whether the shaft is turning fast, turning slowly or held still. The current through that wire is very different in each case, however, because a motor is also a generator, and a turning shaft produces a voltage that opposes the supply.

That fact, together with the rule that torque is proportional to current, fixes a motor's whole behaviour as a straight line between two ends, stall, where the shaft is held still, and no load, where it turns freely.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to compute the stall current, the no-load speed and the current and torque at a given speed for a DC motor.
intro.whyItMatters: Choosing and driving a motor depends on knowing how much current and torque it gives at each speed.

recap.keyIdea: A DC motor makes torque in proportion to current and back-EMF in proportion to speed, so its current is largest at stall and falls as it turns.

blocks.text: With T = Kt I, E = Ke ω and I = (V − E) / R, the motor of this lesson draws 6 A at stall and gives 0.30 N m, turns at 240 rad/s with no load, and sits on a straight line between the two. Its mechanical power peaks at half the no-load speed, 18 W, and a stalled motor turns all of its power into heat.
A catalogue's rpm must be converted to rad/s before use.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson controls such a motor's speed by switching its supply on and off quickly with PWM.

lessons.title: Driving a motor: PWM and H-bridges

reveal.text: Half of the time at 12 V and half at 0 V averages to 6 V, so the fraction of each period for which the switch is on sets the voltage the motor sees.

lead.text: To run a motor at half voltage from a 12 V supply the simplest idea is a resistor in series, which drops half the voltage. With a motor current of 3 A that resistor has 6 V across it and carries 3 A, so it wastes 6 V × 3 A = 18 W as heat, which is as much as the motor delivers and more than a small resistor can survive.

The remedy is not to lower the voltage but to switch it. A transistor used as a switch is either fully on, with almost no voltage across it, or fully off, with no current through it, and in both states the power it wastes is close to zero. Turning the full supply on and off fast enough, the motor sees only the *average*.

afterFigure.text: Fast switching of this kind is called **pulse-width modulation**, or PWM. The fraction of each period for which the switch is on is the **duty cycle**, and it is the control knob: the average voltage is the duty cycle times the supply, so the 12 V supply at 25% duty gives 3 V on average, at 50% gives 6 V and at 75% gives 9 V.

diagram.alt: A 12 volt square wave that is on for part of each period. Three cases use duty cycles of 25, 50 and 75 percent, with the average of 3, 6 and 9 volts drawn as a dashed line.
diagram.caption: The supply is switched fully on and off. The average is the duty cycle times the supply. Use the buttons to change the duty.

reveal.text: The relation is linear: doubling the duty cycle doubles the average, which makes the speed easy to set from a program.

lead.text: The motor does not respond to each pulse because its winding is an **inductor**, which resists any sudden change in current. The current builds up and decays over a time of about L / R, called the **time constant**. For a winding of 1 mH and 2 Ω this is 1 mH / 2 Ω = 0.5 ms.

If the switching period is much shorter than that, say 50 µs, which is a switching frequency of 20 kHz, the current has no time to move far during one pulse and stays close to its average. With a 50 µs period it stays within 0.2 A of the average 3 A. With a 5 ms period, ten times the time constant, the current rises and falls nearly the whole way with every pulse and the motor jerks. A frequency of about 20 kHz is also above hearing, so the motor does not whine.

diagram.alt: The current in a motor winding of 1 millihenry and 2 ohms switched at 50 percent duty from 12 volts. A 50 microsecond period gives an almost steady 3 amps. A 5 millisecond period makes the current swing between nearly 0 and 6 amps.
diagram.caption: A short switching period is smoothed by the winding, and a long one is not. Use the buttons to compare.

reveal.text: A switching period many times shorter than this value gives a steady current, so a larger time constant allows a lower switching frequency.

lead.text: A single switch drives a motor one way only. To reverse it the supply must be connected the other way round, which an **H-bridge** does with four switches, two on each side of the motor, in the shape of the letter H. The top switches, Q1 and Q2, connect to the supply and the bottom ones, Q3 and Q4, to ground. Turning on Q1 and Q4 sends current through the motor from left to right. PWM is applied to one switch of the pair to set the speed.

Turning on both bottom switches joins the two motor terminals to ground, and the spinning motor, which is a generator, brakes itself against its own back-EMF. What must never happen is for the two switches on one side to be on together, as in the last case of the figure. That joins the supply directly to ground, through no load, in a fault called **shoot-through**, and the current is limited only by the switches' resistance, which destroys them.

afterFigure.text: Because the winding is an inductor, the current in it cannot stop at once when the switches turn off. Each switch therefore has a **diode** in parallel, usually built in, giving the current a path back to the supply. Without those diodes the collapsing current would push the voltage at the switches to a level that destroys them.

diagram.alt: An H-bridge: four switches Q1 and Q2 at the top and Q3 and Q4 at the bottom, with the motor across the middle. Three cases show forward, brake and the forbidden short circuit, with the current path highlighted.
diagram.caption: The two top switches connect to the supply and the two bottom ones to ground. Use the buttons to see each setting.

reveal.text: Reverse uses the other diagonal of the bridge, so the current crosses the motor in the opposite direction.

lead.text: A transistor that is fully on is not a perfect conductor but a resistor of a few tens of milliohms, called **Rds(on)**, and the current through it wastes I² × Rds(on) as heat. For 3 A through 30 mΩ this is 9 × 0.03 = 0.27 W, which is less than a sixtieth of the 18 W that the series resistor wasted. In a bridge the current passes through two switches, one at the top and one at the bottom, so the loss is twice that.

The loss grows with the *square* of the current, so doubling the current quadruples the heat. It is the reason a motor driver specifies a current rating, and why the switches in a driver for a larger motor need a heat sink, or a lower Rds(on).

steps.headline: A switch with Rds(on) = 20 mΩ carries 3 A. How much power does it waste, and how much do the two switches of a bridge waste?

workedSteps.text: Convert the resistance to ohms.
The power in one switch is the current squared times its resistance.
The same current passes through two switches in a bridge, so double it.

steps.headline: A switch with Rds(on) = 10 mΩ carries 5 A. How much power does it waste?

workedSteps.text: Convert the resistance to ohms.
The power in one switch is the current squared times its resistance.

reveal.text: Compared with the 18 W a series resistor wasted in the first example, the switches waste only 0.48 W, which is why drivers are built this way.

lessons.orientation: How PWM sets the average voltage, why the motor smooths it, how an H-bridge reverses a motor and what the switches waste.
lessons.reviewLabel: Driving a motor: PWM and H-bridges

blocks.text: A 12 V motor can be slowed by putting a resistor in series with it, but at half speed the resistor turns about as much power into heat as the motor turns into motion. Motor drivers do something else, switching the full supply on and off, typically 20,000 times a second, and the motor responds to the average voltage, which is set by the fraction of each period for which the switch is on.
The motor can follow that average because its winding resists sudden changes in current, and a bridge of four such switches lets the same drive turn it in either direction or brake it.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to compute the average voltage of a PWM signal, find the power a switch wastes and say which switches an H-bridge turns on for each direction.
intro.whyItMatters: Nearly every motor on a robot is driven by PWM through a bridge, so its average voltage and its heat both come from these formulas.

recap.keyIdea: PWM sets a motor's average voltage to duty × supply with almost no waste, and an H-bridge reverses it as long as one side's switches are never on together.

blocks.text: The motor's winding smooths the switched current when the period is far shorter than L / R, so it responds to D × V, and the switches waste only I² × Rds(on), 0.18 W for 3 A through 20 mΩ. An H-bridge turns on Q1 and Q4 for one direction and Q2 and Q3 for the other, with the diodes carrying the winding's current when the switches turn off.
Turning on both switches of one side is shoot-through, a short circuit.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson turns to motors that move by a fixed angle, steppers, and to servos that hold a position.

lessons.title: Steppers and servos

lead.text: A **stepper motor** has several coils around a toothed rotor. Switching on one coil pulls the nearest tooth of the rotor to it, switching it off and the next one on pulls the rotor on, and each change of coil is one **step**. A common stepper has 200 steps per revolution, so one step is 360° / 200 = 1.8°.

The great convenience is that a controller does not have to measure the position. It *counts* the steps it has commanded, and 100 steps is 180° from where the motor started. The controller sets the speed as well, since a step rate of 200 steps per second is one revolution per second.

afterFigure.text: The price of counting is that the position is never checked. A stepper run **open loop**, with no sensor, assumes that every step happened. If the load is too heavy, or the step rate rises too fast for the rotor to follow, steps are skipped, and the controller goes on counting with an error that nothing reports.

diagram.alt: Four coils around a rotor. Switching on one coil after another turns the rotor to face each in turn, one step at a time. A real stepper has 200 steps per turn, 1.8 degrees each.
diagram.caption: The coil that is switched on pulls the rotor to it. Use the buttons to step round.

A real motor has 200, of 1.8° each.</text></svg>

reveal.text: 120 revolutions a minute is 2 a second, and each revolution takes 200 steps, so the rate is 400 steps a second.

lead.text: The step rate follows from the speed. Divide the revolutions per minute by 60 to get revolutions per second, and multiply by the steps per revolution. At 900 rpm with 200 full steps per revolution the rate is 15 × 200 = 3000 steps per second.

A driver can also share the current between two coils in unequal amounts, which places the rotor *between* the full step positions. This is **microstepping**, and with 16 microsteps per full step the motor has 200 × 16 = 3200 steps per revolution, each of 0.1125°. The commands are finer, and the motion is smoother and quieter, but the accuracy is not 16 times better: the torque that holds the rotor on a microstep is small, and friction can leave it a little short. The step rate for the same 900 rpm is 16 times higher, 48,000 steps per second.

steps.headline: How many steps per second does a 200-step motor need to turn at 600 rpm, and how many with 16× microstepping?

workedSteps.text: Convert the speed to revolutions per second.
Multiply by the steps per revolution.
With 16× microstepping there are 16 times as many steps for each revolution.

reveal.text: The controller can only send steps as fast as its timer allows, so a high microstepping setting limits the top speed.

lead.text: A stepper's rotation becomes a straight-line motion through a **lead screw**, a threaded rod that moves a nut forward by its **lead**, the distance for one turn. With a lead of 8 mm and 3200 steps per revolution, one step moves the nut 8 / 3200 = 0.0025 mm, which is 2.5 µm.

That figure is the *resolution* of the command, the smallest move the controller can ask for. It says nothing about accuracy, which depends on the screw, the loads, and any steps that were skipped. The same arithmetic gives the speed: a motor at 2 revolutions per second on an 8 mm lead moves the nut 16 mm every second.

A **servo** is a motor with feedback. Inside a hobby servo are a small DC motor, a gearbox, a potentiometer on the output shaft that measures its angle, and a circuit that drives the motor until the measured angle matches the wanted one. The controller therefore does not count anything: it sends the angle it wants and the servo holds it.

The angle is sent as the *width* of a pulse. By convention the pulse repeats every 20 ms, and its width runs from 1 ms for one end of the range to 2 ms for the other, taken in this lesson as 0° to 180°, so the angle is (pulse − 1 ms) × 180° per millisecond. A pulse of 1.25 ms means 45°. The range varies from one servo to another, and many common servos turn through only about 90° as the pulse goes from 1 ms to 2 ms, so the numbers here are a convention, not a promise.

afterFigure.text: The width sets the *position*, not the speed. A longer pulse does not make the horn turn faster, and a servo moves to its new angle as fast as its motor allows.

diagram.alt: A servo command: a pulse of 1 to 2 milliseconds repeated every 20 milliseconds. The pulse width sets the angle of the servo horn: 1 ms gives 0 degrees, 1.25 ms gives 45 degrees and 2 ms gives 180 degrees.
diagram.caption: The width of the pulse sets the angle, not the speed. Use the buttons to change the pulse.

reveal.text: The pulse width maps linearly onto the angle, so the quarter of the way from 2 ms is a quarter of the range back from 180°.
The speed is the revolutions per second times the lead, so doubling the step rate doubles the speed.
Open-loop control cannot see a lost step, so a design either leaves a margin of torque or adds an encoder.

lessons.orientation: How a stepper's steps and a servo's pulse width turn into position, speed and distance.
lessons.nextAction: Compute the torque a wheel needs and choose a gearbox ratio and motor.

blocks.text: A 3D printer moves its nozzle to within a few hundredths of a millimetre, and its controller does it without ever looking. It counts instead: a motor of 200 steps per revolution, microstepped 16 times and turning a screw with an 8 mm lead, moves the carriage 0.0025 mm for each step it commands, so the position is known from the number of steps sent.

A hobby servo works the other way, because it looks and does not count. It carries its own position sensor and feedback loop, and the controller tells it only the angle to hold, coded in the width of a pulse.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to find a stepper's step rate and the travel of a lead screw, and map a servo's angle to its pulse width.
intro.whyItMatters: Most small mechanisms in robots are positioned by one of these two motors, and the conversions are the same each time.

recap.keyIdea: A stepper is positioned by counting steps, a servo by a pulse width that sets its angle, and the first is open loop and the second closed.

blocks.text: The step rate is revolutions per second times steps per revolution, and a lead screw divides its lead by the steps to give the distance for one step. A hobby servo maps a 1 to 2 ms pulse onto an angle, conventionally 0° to 180°, and the width sets the position, not the speed.
Microstepping makes the commands finer but not the accuracy, and a stepper that is overloaded can lose steps without telling anyone.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson sizes a motor and gearbox for a wheel, starting from the torque the load needs.

lessons.title: Sizing a motor and gearbox

lead.text: A motor is chosen for what it must do, and the way to start is to write the job down: the robot's mass, the steepest slope it must climb, the speed it must reach and the radius of its wheels.

On a slope of angle θ, the weight m g has a part that pulls the robot back down the slope, *m g sin θ*. The drive must supply an equal force just to hold the robot there, and more to climb. For a 6 kg robot, with g = 9.81 m/s², the weight is 58.9 N, and on a slope of 10° the force needed is 58.9 × sin 10° = 10.22 N. Rolling resistance and acceleration are left out, and are covered by the margin that is added at the end.

afterFigure.text: This is the force for the *whole robot*. A robot usually has more than one driven wheel, and the next screens work with the force at one of them.

diagram.alt: A 6 kilogram robot on a slope of 5, 10 or 20 degrees. The weight of 58.9 newtons acts straight down, and the force needed to hold or climb the slope is the weight times the sine of the angle: 5.13, 10.22 and 20.13 newtons.
diagram.caption: A steeper slope needs more force along it. Use the buttons to change the angle.

reveal.text: Dividing the total between the four driven wheels gives each one a quarter, which is the force each wheel's torque must produce at the ground.

lead.text: Each driven wheel has to push the ground with a force F, and the motor must give it the matching torque: *wheel torque = F × r*, with r the wheel radius in metres. With 4 N per wheel and r = 0.06 m, each wheel needs 4 × 0.06 = 0.24 N m. The torque grows with the radius, so a bigger wheel needs a stronger motor for the same push.

The speed goes the other way. A robot at speed v on wheels of radius r has wheels turning at ω = v / r. At 0.5 m/s and 0.05 m that is 10 rad/s, or 10 × 60 / 2π = 95.5 rpm. A motor is rarely well suited to turn so slowly and so strongly, because a small motor turns at thousands of rpm with very little torque, and a gearbox between the two makes up the difference.

steps.headline: A 6 kg robot with two driven wheels of radius 0.05 m must hold a 10° slope. What torque does each wheel need?

workedSteps.text: Find the force along the slope.
Share it between the two driven wheels.
Multiply by the wheel radius to get the torque at each wheel.

steps.headline: A 4 kg robot with two driven wheels of radius 0.04 m must hold a 15° slope. What torque does each wheel need?

workedSteps.text: Find the force along the slope.
Share it between the two driven wheels.
The torque at a wheel is the force it supplies multiplied by the wheel radius.

lead.text: A **gearbox** with ratio *N* turns its output N times slower than its input, and the torque at the output is larger by about the same factor. The **gear ratio** is therefore the motor speed divided by the wheel speed. A motor that turns at 3000 rpm driving a wheel that must turn at 95.5 rpm needs a ratio of 3000 / 95.5 = 31.4, and since gearboxes come in round ratios a designer picks 30:1.

A ratio of 10:1 gives a fast wheel of 300 rpm, and 50:1 a wheel of 60 rpm that is much stronger. Every gear mesh also loses some energy to friction, so the torque is multiplied by the ratio times the **efficiency**, which for the 80% box of the figure is 0.8 × N.

afterFigure.text: A high ratio makes the robot strong and slow and a low one fast and weak, and the right ratio is the one that gives the speed wanted with the motor running near its best.

diagram.alt: A motor at 3000 revolutions per minute driving a wheel through a gearbox with 80 percent efficiency. Three cases with ratios 10, 20 and 50 show the wheel speed falling to 300, 150 and 60 rpm while the torque multiplier rises to 8, 16 and 40.
diagram.caption: A larger ratio gives a slower wheel and a stronger one. Use the buttons to change the ratio.

reveal.text: Round to the nearest ratio the gearbox is sold in, and then re-check the speed and torque with that figure.

lead.text: Working back from the wheel, the motor's torque is *wheel torque / (ratio × efficiency)*. For a wheel torque of 0.2555 N m, a ratio of 30 and an efficiency of 0.8, the motor torque is 0.2555 / 24 = 0.01065 N m, or 10.6 mN m. A designer who left the efficiency out would find 8.5 mN m, which is 20% too small, and the robot would stall on the slope.

The calculation uses ideal conditions, so the result is multiplied by a margin of about 2, which allows for rolling resistance, acceleration, a rough floor and a battery that is not full. A motor torque of 10.6 mN m becomes a requirement of about 21 mN m. The last check is the electrical one: with a torque constant Kt = 0.05 N m/A, 21 mN m needs a current of 0.021 / 0.05 = 0.42 A, which the motor driver must be able to supply, and the stall current of the motor, found as in the lesson on DC motors, must stay inside the driver's rating.

reveal.text: The product of ratio and efficiency is the true torque gain, which is less than the ratio alone.
The driver must supply this current continuously, so it is the figure that decides whether the driver is large enough.
Speed and torque are separate requirements, so a drive must be checked against the steepest slope as well as against the speed.

lessons.orientation: How to size a motor and gearbox from the job a wheel has to do.
lessons.nextAction: Compute where the hand of a two-link robot arm is, from its joint angles.

blocks.text: A 6 kg robot weighs 58.9 N, and on a slope of 10° the part of that weight pulling it back down is 58.9 N × sin 10° = 10.22 N, which the drive has to supply whether or not the robot moves. That force is shared between the driven wheels, turned into a torque by the wheel radius, and then reduced by a gearbox to something a small motor can supply.
A robot sized only for its top speed is quick on the flat and stops at the first ramp, so a drive is worked out backwards, from the force the wheels must push with to the torque the motor must give.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to find the torque a wheel needs, choose a gear ratio and compute the motor torque after the gearbox's efficiency.
intro.whyItMatters: A motor that cannot give the torque on the steepest slope is the commonest reason for a robot that works on the bench and fails outdoors.

recap.keyIdea: The wheel torque comes from the slope force and the radius, and the motor torque is that divided by the ratio and the efficiency, with a margin.

blocks.text: For a 6 kg robot on 10° the force is 10.22 N, 5.11 N for each of two wheels, and the wheel torque is 0.256 N m at r = 0.05 m. A 30:1 gearbox of efficiency 0.8 brings the motor torque to 10.6 mN m, and a margin of about 2 gives a requirement near 21 mN m.
The gear ratio is the motor speed divided by the wheel speed, and the driver must be able to supply the stall current of the motor chosen.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson begins the third module, on robot geometry, with the position of an arm's hand from its joint angles.

lessons.title: Arms: where is the hand?

lead.text: A robot arm is a chain of rigid **links** joined by **joints**, and the question of where its hand is, given the angles of its joints, is called **forward kinematics**. The simplest useful case has two links in a plane. The base is the origin, the x axis points along the floor, and each joint angle is measured from the line of the *previous* link, so that θ1 is measured from the x axis and θ2 from the direction in which link 1 points.

The elbow is the end of link 1, a distance l1 from the base at angle θ1, so its position is *(l1 cos θ1, l1 sin θ1)*. With l1 = 0.40 m and θ1 = 60°, that is (0.40 × 0.5, 0.40 × 0.866) = (0.200, 0.346) m.

afterFigure.text: The [[cosine and sine|The horizontal and vertical parts of a length that points at an angle.]] are only the horizontal and vertical parts of a length at an angle, and the same pair gives the second link's part when its angle is known.

diagram.alt: A two-link arm with the base at the origin. Link 1 of 0.40 metres is at 60 degrees, and link 2 of 0.25 metres turns minus 30 degrees from it, pointing at 30 degrees from the x axis. The elbow is at 0.200, 0.346 and the hand at 0.417, 0.471.
diagram.caption: The elbow follows from link 1 alone, and the hand adds link 2 at the sum of the two angles. Use the buttons to build the arm.

reveal.text: The relative angles add: 50° + 40° = 90°. This is the angle that link 2's own cosine and sine must use.

lead.text: The second link starts at the elbow and is l2 long. It points at the angle of link 1 *plus* the elbow bend, θ1 + θ2, because the joint angle was measured from link 1. Beginners often use θ2 alone, which would be correct only if θ2 were measured from the x axis; a joint angle is **relative** and the direction of the link in the world is **absolute**, and the sum turns one into the other.

The hand is therefore at *x = l1 cos θ1 + l2 cos(θ1 + θ2)* and *y = l1 sin θ1 + l2 sin(θ1 + θ2)*. In the arm drawn at the start of the lesson, with l2 = 0.25 m and θ2 = −30°, the second link points at 30° and adds (0.25 cos 30°, 0.25 sin 30°) = (0.217, 0.125) to the elbow, giving the hand at (0.417, 0.471) m.
These two lines are all of forward kinematics for a planar two-link arm. For longer arms the angles keep adding, one term for each link.

steps.headline: An arm has l1 = 0.40 m and l2 = 0.25 m, with θ1 = 40° and θ2 = 35°. Where is the hand?

workedSteps.text: The first link points at θ1, so the elbow is at
The second link points at the sum of the angles.
It adds its own length at that angle to the elbow.
Add the two parts.

steps.headline: An arm has l1 = 0.30 m and l2 = 0.20 m, with θ1 = 45° and θ2 = 90°. Where is the hand?

workedSteps.text: The elbow is at (0.30 cos 45°, 0.30 sin 45°).
The second link adds its own length at the sum of the two joint angles.
Adding that part to the elbow's position gives the hand.

reveal.text: With θ1 = 0 the angles add to 90°, so link 2 points straight up and contributes all of its length to y.

lead.text: The distance of the hand from the base depends on the elbow angle. With the arm stretched straight the links add, and the **reach** is l1 + l2, 0.3 + 0.2 = 0.5 m. With the elbow folded right back, so that the second link doubles back over the first, the links subtract, and the reach is |l1 − l2| = 0.1 m. Every elbow angle in between gives a reach between those two values.

Rotating the whole arm about the base sweeps those distances round every direction. The set of all points the hand can reach is the **workspace**, and for two links of different lengths it is a *ring* between radius 0.1 m and radius 0.5 m, not a full disc. The points within 0.1 m of the base form a hole that the arm cannot reach.

afterFigure.text: Real joints cannot turn through every angle. A motor mount, a wire or a mechanical stop limits each one, and a limited joint trims the ring to part of its circumference. A target that lies inside the ring may still be out of reach, so the limits have to be checked as well as the distance.

diagram.alt: The reachable region of an arm with links of 0.3 and 0.2 metres. Stretched out the hand is 0.5 metres from the base, folded back it is 0.1 metres, and over all joint angles the region is a ring between those radii. A fourth case shows joint limits trimming the ring.
